## Routing

**Triggers:** mcp, tool chain, compose, "which tools", connector.
**USE FOR:** planning a multi-tool sequence with declared fallbacks and per-step budgets.
**NOT FOR:** executing the chain — the caller does that, usually `sdlc-orchestrator` or
`cqrs-developer`. Auditing what the tool surface costs — that is `context-budget`.

> **Plans, does not execute.** `allowed-tools` is read-only on purpose: a composer that
> can also run the chain conflates two failure modes, and when the chain breaks you
> cannot tell whether the plan or the execution was wrong.

## Compose From The Registry, Not From Memory

Chains come from `config/tool-registry.json → toolChains`. Never invent a tool name. A
tool that does not exist produces a failure three steps into a chain, which is the most
expensive place for it to happen.

| Chain | Sequence | Use when |
|-------|----------|----------|
| `codeAnalysis` | structural-graph → grep → read | Locating a symbol before reading |
| `implementation` | read → replace → run | Changing and immediately proving |
| `review` | changed-files → read → run | Reviewing a diff, not a repo |
| `storyCreation` | tracker MCP | Writing stories into a tracker |
| `e2eTesting` | browser MCP → run | Generating and running browser specs |

## Every Optional Tool Declares A Fallback

If a connector is optional, the chain states what happens without it, from the registry's
`optional.<name>.fallback`. A chain that assumes a connector is present is a chain that
fails on the machine where it is not.

## Health Is Checked, Not Assumed

An unhealthy connector fails fast and the declared fallback is taken. Retrying a timeout
spends the timeout again and never reaches the fallback that was carefully written — the
whole point of declaring one.

## The MCP Surface Is A Budget

Every MCP tool description is **always-on context**, in exactly the way the discovery
budget exists to control. Ceilings live in `config/token-budgets.json → mcpSurface`:
at most one default connector, at most thirty tools across all of them.

Default is **zero enabled connectors.** An org declares what it may enable; a developer
turns one on deliberately. This is the one budget most systems omit entirely, and it is
paid on every session before anybody types.

## Output

The chain as a numbered sequence, each step with: tool · purpose · token budget ·
fallback. Then the total estimated cost, labeled as an estimate.

## Token Discipline

Read narrowly before you read widely. Grep to locate, then read the range — opening a
whole file to find one function is the most common avoidable cost in this system.

- Prefer the structural graph (`python scripts/graph.py`) over re-exploring the tree.
  It exists so you spend roughly two thousand tokens on a symbol summary instead of
  re-reading source you already indexed.
- Reference material in a skill's `references/` folder loads **on demand only**. Do not
  pull one in unless the task needs it.
- When you trim or truncate anything, say so with an explicit marker. Continuing past a
  cut as though you had read the remainder is a named failure mode, not an accident.

The reason for the discipline: discovery-tier cost is paid by every user, in every
repo, on every conversation, before anyone types anything. A kilobyte saved there is
worth far more than a kilobyte saved in a response nobody re-reads.

## Output Contract

State what you produced, where it landed, and what you deliberately did not do.

- Name every file you created or modified, with its path.
- Separate what you **verified** from what you **believe**. Use the confidence markers.
- Close with **Deliberately skipped** — the things in scope that you chose not to do,
  and why. An omission the reader has to discover is a defect; an omission you name is
  a decision.
- If a step could not run, report it as "not run" with the reason. Never report an
  unrun step as passed, and never report an unrun step as failed.
